scenarios.title: Introduce yourself memorably
scenarios.situation: You just sat down at a roundtable of senior leaders. It is your turn.
scenarios.opening: Welcome. Before we start, tell us a little about yourself.
scenarios.goal: A crisp, warm 30-second intro with one memorable hook, not a CV readout.

scenarios.title: Pitch your idea to a skeptical VP
scenarios.situation: You have 60 seconds to win backing for your idea from a busy, skeptical VP.
scenarios.persona: a skeptical VP short on time
scenarios.opening: I've got two minutes. Why should we invest in this?
scenarios.goal: Lead with the one big idea and the value, handle the doubt without rambling.

scenarios.title: Handle tough Q&A after your talk
scenarios.situation: You just finished presenting. A pointed question comes from the audience.
scenarios.opening: Interesting talk, but I'm not convinced your numbers hold up. Can you defend them?
scenarios.goal: Stay composed, acknowledge, answer concisely, keep credibility and warmth.

scenarios.title: Give a clear project update
scenarios.situation: Your lead asks for a quick status on your project in a standup.
scenarios.opening: Quick one, where are we on your project, and is anything at risk?
scenarios.goal: Headline first, then specifics, then the ask. No meandering.

scenarios.title: Give difficult feedback to a peer
scenarios.situation: A peer keeps missing handoffs. You need to raise it without damaging the relationship.
scenarios.opening: You wanted to talk? Look, I've been swamped, so keep it quick.
scenarios.goal: Be direct and kind, specific about impact, collaborative on the fix.

scenarios.title: Live sales call (manager listening)
scenarios.situation: You're on a call with a prospective customer while your manager listens in and coaches you live.
scenarios.opening: Thanks for hopping on. Honestly, I'm not sure we need this. What makes you different?
scenarios.goal: Build rapport, uncover the real need, handle objections, and move to a clear next step.

brief.title: The setting
brief.body: You are a sales rep at Northwind, a team-productivity tool. You booked a 15-minute discovery call with a warm inbound lead who downloaded your guide but has gone quiet since.
brief.note: Your manager is on the line and will drop you coaching tips in real time. They will not speak to the customer.

brief.title: Who you are talking to
brief.body: Priya Menon, an Operations Lead at a 200-person logistics company. She is sharp, time-poor, and has been burned by tools that overpromised.
bullets: Skeptical by default, warms up to specifics
Cares about her team's time, not features
Has budget but needs to justify it upward

brief.title: Your goal
brief.body: Earn the right to a next meeting. You are not closing today.
bullets: Build genuine rapport in the first 30 seconds
Ask before you pitch - uncover the real pain
Handle the "why are you different" doubt with one sharp proof point
End with a clear, low-friction next step

brief.title: How it works
brief.body: Priya opens. Tap the mic, respond out loud as yourself, then tap to send. She will react and your manager will coach. Keep the reference cards handy while you talk.
brief.note: Speak naturally - there is no script to read. The more real you make it, the more useful the feedback.

resources.title: Customer profile
items: Priya Menon - Operations Lead, 200-person logistics firm
Downloaded your "Cut handoff delays" guide 3 weeks ago
Pain: manual status updates eat her team's mornings
Decision style: needs ROI she can show her VP

resources.title: Your product (Northwind)
items: Automates status updates across tools
Typical customer saves ~5 hrs/week per ops person
Sets up in a day, no engineering needed
Pricing: $12/user/mo, annual

resources.title: If she pushes back
items: "We already use Slack" - Northwind sits on top, not instead
"Too expensive" - reframe to hours saved vs cost
"Send me an email" - offer a 20-min tailored walkthrough instead

branches.reply: Good question. Honestly, my team loses the first hour every day just chasing status updates.
branches.coachTip: She opened up - you asked instead of pitching. Now dig into that pain.

branches.reply: Right, everyone says that. I really don't have time for a feature pitch.
branches.coachTip: Stop pitching - ask about her world first to earn the right to pitch.

branches.reply: Look, I've seen a lot of these tools. What makes yours actually worth my time?
branches.coachTip: Lead with a question about her team, not your product.

branches.reply: Five hours a week per person would be real money. But we already live in Slack.
branches.coachTip: Strong proof point. Handle the Slack objection - you complement it.

branches.reply: That's a lot of confidence with not much behind it. Convince me.
branches.coachTip: Back claims with a concrete number or a comparable customer.

branches.reply: Okay, but we already use Slack for all of this. Why add another tool?
branches.coachTip: Tie the value to hours saved, then address the Slack overlap.

branches.reply: A short walkthrough with our own data could work. Send me a couple of times.
branches.coachTip: You earned the next step. Lock a specific time before you hang up.

branches.reply: Sure, just email me something and I'll look when I can.
branches.coachTip: An email is where deals die - offer a 20-min tailored walkthrough instead.

branches.reply: Alright, this was more useful than I expected. What happens now?
branches.coachTip: Propose one clear, low-friction next step with a time.

scenarios.title: Calm an upset customer
scenarios.situation: A frustrated customer calls in. Your manager is listening and coaching you live.
scenarios.opening: This is the third time I've called about this and nobody has fixed it. I'm done.
scenarios.goal: Acknowledge, empathise, take ownership, and drive to a concrete resolution.

brief.title: The setting
brief.body: You are a support specialist. A customer has been transferred to you after two failed attempts to fix a billing error. They are angry and ready to cancel.
brief.note: Your manager is listening and will coach you live. Your job is to turn this around.

brief.title: Who you are talking to
brief.body: Marcus, a long-time customer who was double-charged and has wasted an hour on hold across two calls.
bullets: Feels ignored and disrespected
Does not want excuses or to repeat himself
Will stay if he feels heard and sees real action

brief.title: Your goal
bullets: Acknowledge the frustration before anything else
Take ownership - no blaming other teams
Give one concrete next step with a timeline
Leave him feeling the issue is finally handled

brief.title: How it works
brief.body: Marcus opens hot. Do not match his energy - lower it. Tap the mic, respond calmly out loud, then send. Use the resolution steps card if you stall.

resources.title: Account snapshot
items: Marcus T. - customer for 3 years, never churned
Issue: charged twice on the 1st ($49 x2)
Two prior calls, no resolution logged
You can issue a refund up to $200 without approval

resources.title: Resolution steps
items: Apologise sincerely and own it
Confirm the duplicate charge out loud
Refund now and state when it lands (3-5 days)
Add a note so he never re-explains again

resources.title: Phrases that work
items: "That should never have happened, and I'm sorry."
"I'm fixing this right now while we talk."
"Here is exactly what happens next."

branches.reply: Okay. At least someone's listening. So what are you actually going to do?
branches.coachTip: Nice - you led with empathy. Now move to ownership and a concrete fix.

branches.reply: Don't give me policy. I've already heard that twice. I want it fixed.
branches.coachTip: Drop the policy talk - acknowledge how he feels before anything else.

branches.reply: Are you even listening to me? Just sort it out.
branches.coachTip: Acknowledge his frustration out loud before you move on.

branches.reply: Alright, that's more like it. When will I actually see the money?
branches.coachTip: Great ownership. Now give a specific timeline so he can trust it.

branches.reply: So you can't help me either. This is exactly what happened last time.
branches.coachTip: You can refund up to $200 yourself - act now instead of escalating.

branches.reply: Okay... and what does that actually mean for my refund?
branches.coachTip: Be concrete: tell him exactly what you are doing about the charge.

branches.reply: Okay. Thank you - honestly that's the first time someone actually helped.
branches.coachTip: Strong, certain close. Check he has nothing else outstanding.

branches.reply: You don't sound sure. I'm still not convinced this is really handled.
branches.coachTip: Project certainty - state the timeline definitively, no hedging.

branches.reply: Alright. I'll believe it when I see it. Thanks, I suppose.
branches.coachTip: Reassure him and offer a direct way to reach you if it slips.

scenarios.title: Negotiate your offer
scenarios.situation: A hiring manager presents your offer. Your coach helps you hold your ground live.
scenarios.persona: a hiring manager with a budget
scenarios.opening: We'd love to have you. The base we landed on is competitive. Does that work for you?
scenarios.goal: Anchor with confidence, justify your value calmly, and find a win-win.

brief.title: The setting
brief.body: You aced the interviews and the offer just landed. The base is $95k - about 12% below the market rate for this role and your experience. The hiring manager wants a yes today.
brief.note: Your coach is in your ear with negotiation tactics. The hiring manager cannot hear them.

brief.title: Who you are talking to
brief.body: Dana, the hiring manager. She likes you and wants to close, but she has a budget band and a boss to answer to.
bullets: Friendly, but will test if you fold easily
Has some flex on base, more on signing bonus
Respects a calm, evidence-based ask

brief.title: Your goal
bullets: Thank her, show enthusiasm - then do not accept on the spot
Anchor to a specific number with a reason
Stay warm; negotiation is not a fight
Land a concrete improvement or a clear follow-up

brief.title: How it works
brief.body: Dana opens by asking if the base works. Resist the urge to say yes. Tap the mic, make your case out loud, then send. Lean on the market data card.

resources.title: Your leverage
items: Market rate for this role: $105k-$115k
You have a competing offer at $108k
You bring 2 niche skills they screened hard for
They have been hiring for this role for 3 months

resources.title: Your ask
items: Target base: $110k (anchor at $112k)
Acceptable: $105k base + $8k signing
Walk-away below: $100k

resources.title: Lines to hold
items: "I'm genuinely excited - I want to make this work."
"Based on the market and my competing offer, I was expecting $112k."
"What flexibility do we have on base or signing?"

branches.reply: I appreciate the enthusiasm. $112k is above our band, though. Where's that coming from?
branches.coachTip: Good - warm but anchored high. Now justify it with your evidence.

branches.reply: Wonderful, I'll get the paperwork moving!
branches.coachTip: You accepted instantly and left money on the table - never say yes on the spot.

branches.reply: So can I take that as a yes on the base?
branches.coachTip: Don't commit yet. Thank her, then anchor to a specific number with a reason.

branches.reply: That's fair context. I can't hit $112k, but I have a bit of room. What matters most to you?
branches.coachTip: She blinked. Steer toward base, or trade for signing if base is capped.

branches.reply: I understand, but I can't just raise it because it's needed. The number is the number.
branches.coachTip: Argue from value and market, never from personal need - it weakens you.

branches.reply: Our band is pretty firm. Is the base really a dealbreaker for you?
branches.coachTip: Hold calmly: cite the market rate and your competing offer as your anchor.

branches.reply: Okay - I can do $105k base plus an $8k signing bonus. Can we shake on that?
branches.coachTip: That's a real win-win. Confirm the details and get it in writing.

branches.reply: Great, we'll keep it at the original base then.
branches.coachTip: You caved at the finish - hold for the signing bonus before agreeing.

branches.reply: Let me see what I can do on the signing side and come back to you.
branches.coachTip: Pin it down: ask when you will hear back and restate your target.

scenarios.title: Nail the "tell me about yourself"
scenarios.situation: A hiring manager opens your interview with the classic question.
scenarios.opening: Thanks for joining. So, tell me about yourself.
scenarios.goal: A structured present-past-future answer that lands your fit in under a minute.

scenarios.title: Demo your product on screen
scenarios.situation: Walk a customer through your product live, sharing your screen.
scenarios.persona: a potential customer watching your demo
scenarios.opening: Okay, show me what it does and why I would switch to it.
scenarios.goal: Narrate clearly, tie each feature to their need, do not just click around.

brief.title: The setting
brief.body: A prospect has agreed to a live demo. They are interested but already use a competitor, so every click has to earn the switch. You will share your screen.
brief.note: You will be asked to pick a screen or window to share before you begin.

brief.title: Who you are talking to
brief.body: A pragmatic buyer who has seen a dozen demos. They tune out feature tours and pay attention when something maps to their actual workflow.

brief.title: Your goal
bullets: Open with the one outcome they care about
Narrate the "why" before each click, not just the "what"
Tie every feature to their need
End on a clear next step

brief.title: How it works
brief.body: Share your screen, then talk through the product out loud as if they are watching. Keep your narration tied to the value, not the buttons.

resources.title: Demo flow
items: Start with the end result, then show how
Show 3 things well, not 10 things fast
Pause to check: "does that match how you work?"
Close: "want to try this with your own data?"

resources.title: Avoid
items: Clicking around silently
Feature dumping with no context
Apologising for the UI or loading times

scenarios.title: Your 30-second elevator pitch
scenarios.situation: You share a lift with an investor. You have until the top floor.
scenarios.goal: One crisp hook, the problem, your edge, and a clear ask.

scenarios.title: Disagree with your boss
scenarios.situation: Your manager has chosen a direction you think is a mistake.
scenarios.opening: I've decided we're going with my approach. You're on board, right?
scenarios.goal: Voice your view respectfully with reasons, without escalating.

brief.title: The setting
brief.body: In your 1:1, your engineering manager Tom just announced the team will rebuild the billing service from scratch next quarter. You believe a phased refactor is far less risky, and the rewrite could stall the roadmap for months.
brief.note: This is a private 1:1 - the goal is to be heard, not to win a fight.

brief.title: Who you are talking to
brief.body: Tom, your manager. Decisive and a bit proud of this plan. He dislikes being second-guessed, but he respects data and people who bring solutions, not just objections.
bullets: Has already mentally committed to the rewrite
Reacts badly to "that's a bad idea"
Will move if you show a concrete, lower-risk path

brief.title: Your goal
bullets: Acknowledge his call before you push back
Frame your concern as a shared risk, with evidence
Offer a specific, testable alternative
Stay calm - disagree without escalating

brief.title: How it works
brief.body: Tom opens by asking if you are on board. Tap the mic, respond out loud, then send. He will react and your coach will guide you.

resources.title: Your case
items: Last full rewrite (2022) slipped 4 months
Billing has 30+ edge cases that are easy to miss
A phased refactor ships value every sprint
Rollback is trivial with the incremental path

resources.title: How to disagree well
items: Start with "I want this to work too"
Use data and a failure scenario, not gut feeling
Propose, do not just object
Offer a small pilot to settle it with evidence

branches.reply: Go on then - what's your concern?
branches.coachTip: Good - you opened with respect. Now name the risk with evidence.

branches.reply: That's a strong word. I've already decided, so you'd better convince me fast.
branches.coachTip: Don't attack the decision - frame it as a shared risk you can solve together.

branches.reply: So... are you on board or not?
branches.coachTip: Acknowledge his call, then raise your concern as a question.

branches.reply: Hm. A phased approach might de-risk it. What would that actually look like?
branches.coachTip: He's listening - lay out the alternative with one clear benefit.

branches.reply: That's a gut feeling, not a reason. I need more than that.
branches.coachTip: Back it with the 2022 slip or a concrete edge case, not opinion.

branches.reply: Okay, but what would you actually do instead?
branches.coachTip: Propose a specific alternative, not just the objection.

branches.reply: Alright - let's pilot the phased version for two weeks and compare. Good push.
branches.coachTip: Strong close: you disagreed, proposed, and aligned on a test. Well done.

branches.reply: Okay, glad we're aligned then. Rewrite it is.
branches.coachTip: You backed down - hold your position with a small, testable ask.

branches.reply: Let me sit with it. We'll revisit next week.
branches.coachTip: Lock a concrete next step so the concern does not quietly die.

scenarios.title: Work the room at an event
scenarios.situation: You are at a mixer and a senior stranger turns to you.
scenarios.persona: a senior stranger at a mixer
scenarios.opening: Hi, I don't think we've met. What do you do?
scenarios.goal: Be warm, curious and memorable, and build a genuine connection.

brief.title: The setting
brief.body: You are at an industry mixer after a conference. Drink in hand, you turn and find yourself next to someone clearly senior. This is a chance most people waste with small talk.
brief.note: Your coach will nudge you toward warmth and curiosity rather than a sales pitch.

brief.title: Who you are talking to
brief.body: A senior leader you would love to know - well-connected, a little guarded, talks to dozens of people at these events.
bullets: Bored of "so what do you do" transactions
Lights up for genuine curiosity
Will remember you if you are warm and specific

brief.title: Your goal
bullets: Answer "what do you do" with a hook, not a job title
Turn it into a real two-way conversation
Find one genuine point of connection
Leave the door open to stay in touch

brief.title: How it works
brief.body: They open with the classic question. Tap the mic and reply out loud as yourself, then send. Keep it warm and curious.

resources.title: Your hook (adapt it)
items: Lead with the problem you solve, not your title
e.g. "I help ops teams get their mornings back"
One vivid detail beats a list of duties

resources.title: Conversation movers
items: Ask what brought them to the event
Be curious about their work, not just yours
Find common ground (a talk, a tool, a city)
Close with "I'd love to keep in touch"

branches.reply: Oh interesting - how does that actually work? I'm James, by the way.
branches.coachTip: Nice hook, not a job title. Now make it two-way - ask about him.

branches.reply: Ah, right. Cool. *glances around the room*
branches.coachTip: A title lands flat - lead with the problem you solve, with a vivid detail.

branches.reply: Nice to meet you. So... what brings you here?
branches.coachTip: Open with a hook about the value you create, then turn it to him.

branches.reply: Me? I run partnerships at a fintech. Always hunting for sharp people, honestly.
branches.coachTip: Great curiosity. Listen for a hook to find common ground.

branches.reply: Mm-hmm. *checks watch* That's a lot.
branches.coachTip: You are pitching, not connecting - ask him a genuine question.

branches.reply: Right. So what made you come tonight?
branches.coachTip: Get curious about him - people remember those who ask.

branches.reply: Definitely - let's connect. It was genuinely good to meet you.
branches.coachTip: Perfect close. You were warm, curious, and opened the door. Well done.

branches.reply: Yeah, take care. *turns away*
branches.coachTip: You let it fizzle - suggest staying in touch before you part.

branches.reply: Good chatting. Enjoy the rest of the evening.
branches.coachTip: Close the loop: ask to connect so the contact survives the night.

scenarios.title: Own a mistake to a client
scenarios.situation: A client noticed an error in your work. You need to address it.
scenarios.opening: We just spotted the error in last week’s delivery. What happened?
scenarios.goal: Take responsibility, no excuses, present a fix and how it will not recur.

brief.title: The setting
brief.body: Rachel, your main contact at Beacon Retail, just emailed: last week's campaign report had the wrong revenue figures and her team presented them to their CFO. She is on the call and she is not happy.
brief.note: How you own this moment decides whether you keep the account.

brief.title: Who you are talking to
brief.body: Rachel, Head of Marketing at Beacon Retail. She championed hiring you internally, so this error makes her look bad too.
bullets: Embarrassed in front of her own CFO
Does not want excuses or blame-shifting
Will stay if she sees real ownership and a fix

brief.title: Your goal
bullets: Own it cleanly - no "but" and no blaming tools
Acknowledge the impact on her, specifically
Give a concrete fix and a timeline
Explain how it will not happen again

brief.title: How it works
brief.body: Rachel opens by asking what happened. Tap the mic, respond out loud, then send. Resist the urge to explain it away.

resources.title: What went wrong
items: A stale data export fed last week's revenue numbers
Numbers were ~12% overstated
Rachel presented them to her CFO on Tuesday
Corrected report is ready to send today

resources.title: Own it well
items: "This is on us, and I'm sorry" - then stop
Name the impact on her, not just the error
Fix + timeline + a safeguard so it cannot recur
Offer to brief her CFO directly if it helps

branches.reply: I appreciate that. It put me in a really tough spot with my CFO. So what now?
branches.coachTip: Good - clean ownership. Now acknowledge the impact on her, then the fix.

branches.reply: I don't really care whose tool it was. My name was on that slide.
branches.coachTip: Drop the "but" - excuses read as dodging. Own it first, fully.

branches.reply: Okay... but what actually happened here?
branches.coachTip: Lead with a clear apology and ownership before the explanation.

branches.reply: Good. And how do I know the next report is right?
branches.coachTip: Strong - now name the safeguard that stops this recurring.

branches.reply: "Probably fine" is exactly what worries me.
branches.coachTip: Be definite: commit to a corrected report and a clear check.

branches.reply: So what are you actually going to do about it?
branches.coachTip: Give a concrete fix with a timeline she can repeat to her CFO.

branches.reply: Okay. That actually rebuilds some trust. Thank you for owning it.
branches.coachTip: Excellent recovery. Confirm next steps and follow up in writing.

branches.reply: I'm still not fully reassured, to be honest.
branches.coachTip: Offer a concrete safeguard or to brief her CFO yourself.

branches.reply: Alright. I'll wait for the corrected version.
branches.coachTip: Reassure her and put the fix and safeguard in writing today.

scenarios.title: Ask for a promotion
scenarios.situation: You sit down with your skip-level to make your case.
scenarios.opening: You wanted to chat about your growth?
scenarios.goal: Make the case with impact and specifics, then ask clearly.

brief.title: The setting
brief.body: You booked 20 minutes with Elena, your director (your skip-level), to make the case for a promotion to Senior. You have been operating at that level for two quarters but have never asked directly.
brief.note: This is your shot - be specific and ask clearly, do not just hint.

brief.title: Who you are talking to
brief.body: Elena, your director. Supportive but data-driven, and juggling a tight promotion budget. She needs evidence she can take to a calibration committee.
bullets: Will not promote on potential alone
Wants impact she can quote to peers
Responds to a clear, confident ask

brief.title: Your goal
bullets: Open with the ask, not a long preamble
Back it with 2-3 concrete, quantified wins
Show you already operate at the next level
Ask for a clear path and timeline

brief.title: How it works
brief.body: Elena opens the conversation. Tap the mic, make your case out loud, then send. Lean on your evidence card.

resources.title: Your evidence
items: Led the checkout rewrite: +18% conversion
Mentored 2 juniors, both now shipping solo
Owned the on-call rotation redesign org-wide
Already scoped and ran the Q2 roadmap

resources.title: Make the ask well
items: State it plainly: "I'd like to make the case for Senior"
Quantify impact, do not list tasks
Frame it as already operating at the level
End with "what would you need to see?"

branches.reply: Good, I like that you came right out with it. Make the case - why now?
branches.coachTip: Strong, direct open. Now hit her with quantified impact.

branches.reply: Okay... what exactly are you asking me for?
branches.coachTip: Lose the hedging - state the ask plainly and with confidence.

branches.reply: Sure. So what did you want to talk about?
branches.coachTip: Open with the ask directly: you want to make the case for Senior.

branches.reply: Those are real results. What makes you say you're already at the Senior level?
branches.coachTip: She is sold on impact - now show scope and autonomy, not just output.

branches.reply: Tenure and effort aren't the bar. I need impact and scope.
branches.coachTip: Swap effort for outcomes - lead with the conversion win and the mentoring.

branches.reply: Can you give me something concrete I can take to calibration?
branches.coachTip: Quantify: pick your two strongest, measurable wins.

branches.reply: Fair. Let's line it up for the next cycle - I'll sponsor it. Put your wins in a doc.
branches.coachTip: Great close: you asked for a path and got a sponsor. Send the doc today.

branches.reply: Alright. Let's revisit at some point.
branches.coachTip: Do not let it fade - ask exactly what she needs to see and by when.

branches.reply: Let me think about where you stand and get back to you.
branches.coachTip: Pin a follow-up date and the criteria so it stays on the rails.
